compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.hw_notes: RTX5090 (Blackwell) has very high memory bandwidth (~1.8 TB/s expected) and large L2 cache. Elementwise ops are trivially parallelizable. The 1M fp16 element tensor is small enough to mostly fit in L2.
compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.notes: Arithmetic intensity is ~0.33 FLOP/byte (1 add / 4 bytes read+written per element pair, fp16). Fully memory-bound; compute is never the limiter.

memory_bandwidth.notes: Dominant bottleneck. Total data movement: 3 * 16*256*256 * 2 bytes = ~6.3 MB per call. Achieving peak bandwidth requires wide vectorized loads/stores (128-bit / half8 or float4) and sufficient in-flight warps.

register_pressure.notes: Trivial kernel; each thread holds at most 4-8 fp16 values in registers at a time. No risk of register spill.

nodes.notes:
ANALYSIS SUMMARY:
• Classification: Pure elementwise (trivial), no reductions, dense contiguous access, output[i] = x[i] + y[i] for all i in [0, 16*256*256=1,048,576).
• Math: z[i] = x[i] + y[i], fp16 arithmetic, each element independent.
• Layout: x,y,z all shape [16,256,256], fp16, row-major contiguous. Flat index suffices.
• Access pattern: Each element read exactly once from x and y, written once to z. Zero reuse opportunity; no shared memory benefit.
• Bottleneck regimes:
  (1) Small grid / undersubscription: too few threads → latency-bound, bandwidth underutilized.
  (2) Non-vectorized loads: scalar half loads waste memory bus width → bandwidth-bound sub-optimally.
  (3) Optimal vectorized path: 128-bit loads (8 fp16 per load), saturating bandwidth → true bandwidth bound.
• Key knobs: vectorization width (1/2/4/8 fp16 per thread per iter), block size, grid size, use of __hadd2 / packed half2 ops.
• Skeleton: flat 1D grid, each thread loads N fp16 values via vector load, adds, stores. No shared memory, no sync.
• RTX5090 (Blackwell): ~1.8 TB/s BW, 170 SMs, warp size 32. Need ~170*4=680 warps in flight minimum to hide latency; 1M/8=128K iterations at width-8 → ~4K warps needed, fits well.
• PyTorch baseline likely already calls cuBLAS/elementwise fused kernel; custom kernel must match or beat via lower overhead and optimal vectorization.

action.description: Implement a flat 1D CUDA kernel that treats the [16,256,256] tensors as a contiguous array of 1,048,576 fp16 elements. Each thread loads 8 fp16 values (128-bit vector load via reinterpret-cast to float4), performs 8 fp16 additions using __hadd2 on packed half2 pairs, and stores 8 fp16 values with a 128-bit vector store. Grid and block sizes are chosen to saturate SM occupancy. No shared memory used. Handles tail elements with scalar fallback if total elements not divisible by 8.
action.rationale: Vectorized 128-bit loads are the canonical approach to saturate memory bandwidth for simple elementwise kernels. Using half2 SIMD addition reduces instruction count. This should achieve close to peak bandwidth utilization on Blackwell.
action.title: Vectorized fp16 elementwise add (128-bit loads, half2 arithmetic)

compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.hw_notes: RTX5090 Blackwell: 128-bit aligned loads match L2/DRAM burst granularity. half2 intrinsics map to native 2-way SIMD fp16 add instructions. 8 elements/thread at 1M elements → 128K threads minimum, well above SM saturation threshold.
compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.notes: Maximally exploits memory-level parallelism. Arithmetic intensity unchanged but memory efficiency improves from 16-bit to 128-bit transactions.
compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.risk: low - alignment guaranteed since tensors from get_inputs() are freshly allocated and contiguous

memory_bandwidth.notes: 128-bit vector loads/stores give 8x fewer memory transactions vs scalar. Expected to reach 90%+ of peak BW. Total 6.3 MB moved; at ~1.8 TB/s this is ~3.5 microseconds theoretically.

register_pressure.notes: ~6 registers per thread (3 float4 regs for x,y,z vectors + index). Extremely low, enabling maximum occupancy.

nodes.notes:
CURRENT:
  does: Loads 2x float4 (16 fp16) per thread iteration using __ldg, performs __hadd2 SIMD additions, writes back 2x float4; handles scalar tail.
  bottleneck: Memory bandwidth dominated; kernel is at ~88.5% of baseline latency (1.13x speedup). Small tensor size (1M fp16 elements) means launch overhead and occupancy limits constrain further gains.
FOLLOW_THROUGH:
  aligned_with_intent: yes
UPDATE_BELIEF:
  Achieved 1.13x speedup vs baseline (0.0067ms vs 0.0076ms). The gain is real but modest — for a 1M-element fp16 add, the kernel is already near memory-bandwidth saturation at small sizes; launch overhead is non-negligible.
  next bet: Try persistent/cooperative kernel with warp-level pipelining or increase elements-per-thread further (process 4x float4 = 32 fp16 per thread) to amortize launch overhead and improve L2 hit rate.
PERF_GAP:
  expected_vs_baseline_factor=0.70 vs observed=0.885 (speedup 1.13x vs predicted ~1.43x).
  Hypothesized reason: At this small tensor size (1M fp16 = 2MB), the kernel is latency-bound by launch overhead and L2/DRAM round-trips rather than peak bandwidth; the 2x float4 unrolling helped but the grid is already compact (256 blocks x 256 threads), so compute-side savings are small.
SELF_CHECK: This node uses 128-bit vectorized loads with half2 arithmetic as its defining strategy. Children should be refinements of this approach.

action.description: Implement a simple scalar fp16 elementwise add kernel as a correctness baseline. Each thread handles one fp16 element using __hadd(). Flat 1D indexing. No vectorization. Block size 256, grid size ceil(N/256). This establishes a correctness-verified baseline to compare against optimized variants.
action.rationale: Scalar kernel is trivially correct and serves as verification baseline. On Blackwell with many SMs, even scalar loads may achieve reasonable BW utilization for this data size, though sub-optimal. Useful as fallback if vectorized version has alignment issues.
action.title: Scalar baseline fp16 elementwise add (no vectorization)

compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.hw_notes: 1M threads at block=256 → 4096 blocks. RTX5090 has ~170 SMs, so ~24 blocks/SM. Adequate occupancy but 16-bit memory transactions are inefficient.
compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.notes: Simple to implement and verify. Under-utilizes memory bus width (16-bit vs 128-bit ideal). Should still be faster than PyTorch overhead if kernel launch cost dominates.

memory_bandwidth.notes: 16-bit scalar loads result in 8x more memory transactions than 128-bit vectorized. Expect 30-50% of peak BW efficiency.
memory_bandwidth.risk: medium - may not beat PyTorch baseline which also uses optimized kernels

register_pressure.notes: Minimal: 2 fp16 input registers + 1 output + 1 index. ~4 registers per thread.

nodes.notes:
SELF_CHECK: This node deliberately avoids vectorization to serve as a simple correctness baseline. Cannot be combined with node_vectorized (which uses 128-bit vector loads) or node_grid_stride (which uses 64-bit vector loads). Mutually exclusive root-child.
De-prioritized: node_vectorized already shows 1.13x speedup over baseline; a scalar kernel is expected to match or underperform baseline. Low exploration value now that a vectorized solution exists.

action.description: Implement a grid-stride loop kernel where each thread processes multiple elements per launch in a strided pattern. Each thread handles elements at indices [tid, tid+gridDim*blockDim, tid+2*gridDim*blockDim, ...] with 64-bit (float2, 4 fp16) vector loads per stride step. Grid is fixed to a small multiple of SM count (e.g., 4*num_SMs blocks) to maximize SM utilization without over-decomposition. This amortizes kernel launch overhead and may improve L2 reuse for larger-than-cache tensors.
action.rationale: Grid-stride loops with fixed small grids can outperform large flat grids by reducing scheduler overhead and improving cache utilization patterns on Blackwell's L2. For 6.3 MB data (fits in L2 ~96MB), a persistent-style kernel may reduce memory latency.
action.title: Grid-stride loop with fixed SM-scaled grid and 64-bit vector loads

compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.hw_notes: RTX5090 ~170 SMs. Fixed grid of 4*170=680 blocks * 256 threads = 174K threads. Each thread processes 1M/174K ≈ 6 elements per grid-stride iteration. 64-bit loads process 4 fp16 per load.
compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.notes: Grid-stride reduces total block count, potentially improving scheduler efficiency. float2 vectorization (64-bit) is a middle ground between scalar and 128-bit.
compute_intensity_and_hw_fit.risk: medium - stride pattern may reduce coalescing efficiency vs flat sequential assignment

memory_bandwidth.notes: 64-bit vector loads give 4x improvement over scalar. For a 6.3 MB working set that likely fits in L2, the stride pattern means L2 cache lines are reused within a warp, which is fine. May approach 80% of peak BW.

register_pressure.notes: Loop over multiple elements: 3 float2 regs for current chunk + loop counter + index. ~8 registers. Still very low.

nodes.notes:
SELF_CHECK: This node uses a grid-stride loop with SM-count-scaled fixed grid and 64-bit (float2) vector loads as its defining strategy. Cannot be combined with node_vectorized (128-bit loads) or node_scalar (no vectorization). Mutually exclusive root-child.
De-prioritized: node_vectorized with 128-bit loads already outperforms at 1.13x speedup. 64-bit loads are inferior to 128-bit for bandwidth saturation on Blackwell. The SM-scaled grid idea is useful but subsumed by the better-performing vectorized approach.

action.title: Increase to 4x float4 (32 fp16) per thread with software pipelining

nodes.notes:
SELF_CHECK: This node refines node_vectorized by doubling the per-thread work (4x float4 = 32 fp16 per thread) to better amortize launch overhead and increase ILP. It is a child refinement, not a sibling alternative.
Intent: Process 4 float4 vectors per thread per iteration (32 fp16 elements). Issue all 4 loads back-to-back before any arithmetic to create a software pipeline that hides L2 latency. Use __ldg for all loads. Halve the grid size accordingly (128 blocks instead of 256). This increases arithmetic intensity per thread and reduces scheduling overhead.
Expected benefit: For a 1M-element tensor, each SM handles more work per warp, reducing tail latency from small-grid effects. The 4x unroll should allow the compiler to better interleave memory and compute ops.
Risk: Register pressure increases; __launch_bounds__ may need adjustment to maintain 4 waves/SM.

kernel_summary: This is a pure elementwise fp16 addition kernel computing z[i] = x[i] + y[i] over 1,048,576 elements (tensor shape [16,256,256]). The operation is embarrassingly parallel with no reductions, no data dependencies, and trivially dense contiguous access. The kernel is fully memory-bandwidth-bound on RTX5090 (Blackwell, ~1.8 TB/s), with arithmetic intensity of ~0.33 FLOP/byte. Total data movement is ~6.3 MB per call, fitting comfortably in L2 cache (~96 MB). The key optimization levers are vectorization width (targeting 128-bit float4/half8 loads to reduce transaction count 8x vs scalar), thread/block geometry to saturate all ~170 SMs, and use of half2 SIMD intrinsics for native 2-wide fp16 add. The main constraint is ensuring aligned 128-bit memory accesses (guaranteed for freshly allocated contiguous tensors) and avoiding kernel launch overhead dominating for this small working set.
open_questions: What is the actual PyTorch baseline latency on RTX5090 for this exact tensor shape? The 6.3 MB working set may already hit the L2 cache making the absolute latency very small (~5-10 us), potentially making kernel launch overhead the dominant term.
Does PyTorch's ATen elementwise kernel already use 128-bit vectorized loads for fp16? If so, a custom kernel must also reduce Python/framework dispatch overhead to show improvement.
What is the RTX5090 (Blackwell) L2 cache size and exact memory bandwidth spec? These determine whether the 6.3 MB working set fits in L2 and what the theoretical floor latency is.
Is __hadd2 (half2 packed add) truly faster than two separate __hadd calls on Blackwell, or does the compiler optimize them equivalently?
How does kernel launch overhead on RTX5090/CUDA 12.x compare to the ~5 us compute time? If launch overhead is 2-3 us, that is a significant fraction of total time.

Are the input tensors guaranteed to be 128-bit aligned (16-byte boundary)? PyTorch typically aligns allocations to at least 256 bytes, so float4 reinterpret should be safe, but this should be verified.
Would using CUDA cooperative groups or __grid_constant__ annotations provide any latency benefit on Blackwell for this trivially simple kernel?
